pages.text: Esenam helped her mother to sort rice. Mixed in the rice were small stones. “Rice and stones are a mixture,” said her mother. “A mixture is two or more things together that are not joined.” Esenam picked out the stones one by one.
sentences: Esenam helped her mother to sort rice.
Mixed in the rice were small stones.
“Rice and stones are a mixture,” said her mother.
“A mixture is two or more things together that are not joined.” Esenam picked out the stones one by one.
pages.alt: On a shaded Ghanaian home veranda, Esenam sits beside her smiling mother picking tiny dark stones out of white rice spread on a wide metal tray.

pages.text: Her cousin Karim brought a sieve. When he shook the rice in it, the small grains fell through and the bigger stones stayed in the sieve. “A sieve separates things of different sizes,” said Karim.
sentences: Her cousin Karim brought a sieve.
When he shook the rice in it, the small grains fell through and the bigger stones stayed in the sieve.
“A sieve separates things of different sizes,” said Karim.
pages.alt: Karim holding a round mesh kitchen sieve over a clean enamel bowl as white grains fall into the bowl and larger pebbles remain on top while Esenam watches.

pages.text: After the rain, they filled a jar with muddy water from a puddle. “Can we drink it?” asked Karim. “No!” said Esenam. “It is dirty. It has soil in it.” The muddy water was a mixture of a solid in a liquid.
sentences: After the rain, they filled a jar with muddy water from a puddle.
“Can we drink it?” asked Karim.
“No!” said Esenam.
“It is dirty.
It has soil in it.” The muddy water was a mixture of a solid in a liquid.
pages.alt: On an outdoor wooden table after rain, Karim sets down a clear glass jar filled with brown muddy puddle water while Esenam shakes her head firmly.

pages.text: They left the jar still for an hour. The soil sank to the bottom, and the water on top looked clearer. Then they poured it slowly through a clean cloth into a bowl. The cloth held back the soil.
sentences: They left the jar still for an hour.
The soil sank to the bottom, and the water on top looked clearer.
Then they poured it slowly through a clean cloth into a bowl.
The cloth held back the soil.
pages.alt: Esenam holding a clean white cotton cloth stretched over a bowl while Karim slowly pours the settled water from the glass jar, leaving dark mud on the cloth.

pages.text: The water looked clear, but their teacher said, “Do not drink it. Germs and other harmful things are too small to see, and the cloth does not remove them. This water is still not safe. Safe drinking water comes from a clean source, or it is boiled or treated by an adult.”
sentences: The water looked clear, but their teacher said, “Do not drink it.
Germs and other harmful things are too small to see, and the cloth does not remove them.
This water is still not safe.
Safe drinking water comes from a clean source, or it is boiled or treated by an adult.”
pages.alt: At school, their female teacher holds up a gentle stop hand beside the bowl of cloth-filtered water on the table while Esenam and Karim listen attentively.

pages.text: Esenam wrote two lessons: “We can separate a mixture by picking, sieving, settling or filtering. And clear water is not always safe water.” Karim wrote, “Always wash your hands after touching dirty water.”

pages.alt: Esenam and Karim sitting side by side at a wooden desk drawing simple icons of a sieve, a jar and clean hands in their notebooks.

activities.question: Why must the children not drink the cloth-filtered water?
options: It may still hold harmful germs

items: Fill a jar with muddy water.
Pour the water slowly through a cloth.
Remember that it is still not safe to drink.
